articles.title: Amazon’s short story collections are one of the best reasons to own a Kindle
articles.summary: Amazon’s publishing label includes a number of excellent short story collections for Kindle owners, including a new series called Magic and Mystery.
articles.body: Over the last few years, I’ve gradually shifted away from ebooks. It’s been part of a general return to physical media, an attempt to create a deeper sense of ownership over the art I love and collect. A Kindle is obviously more convenient than a paperback: It’s tiny, holds a huge library, and you can purchase new books instantly. But, much like with retro game cartridges, I find there’s a deeper connection formed with a book dug out of a stack in a used book shop versus simply choosing the next thing in a series from a menu on an e-reader. But I haven’t completely given up on my Kindle, and there’s one big reason — actually, there are lots of smaller reasons why. Amazon’s Original Stories publishing imprint has steadily curated a huge collection of short story collections, which often feature big-name authors and are particularly great if you’re a fan of genre fiction. The most recent, which came out this week, is called “Magic and Mystery,” and it gathers a bunch of fantasy authors together and has them tackle puzzle box mystery stories, most of which involve a murder of some sort. Like past collections — which have explored everything from the vast expanse of space to straight-up horror — the stories here are incredibly varied, and explore the theme in different and often clever ways. Travis Baldree’s Miss Gentle and the Case of the Very Flat Monk, for instance, introduces a detective character that I absolutely need to see solve other mysteries: an old woman who wears a full suit of armor covered in enchanted human appendages, and who never shows her face. Robert Jackson Bennett’s The Lion’s Tusk, meanwhile, involves a gruesome murder at a royal wedding, and features a clever and incredibly bizarre murder weapon unlike anything I’ve ever seen or read before. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/915LWQmAdLL._SL1500_.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Some of the most impressive stories manage to cram a whole bunch of worldbuilding into a short you can finish in one sitting. Heather Fawcett’s A Labyrinth of Honeybees introduces a fantasy realm rich with a long history of gods and competing religions, while The Wizard Who Kept Himself Suspicious by Scott Lynch convincingly presents an ancient order of magic users who have been friends for centuries, and meet up every 13 years to hang out and show off their skills. There are two great things about these collections. One, obviously, is the stories themselves. I’d recommend all seven shorts in “Magic and Mystery,” and some of my favorite authors have contributed to collections in the past. That includes the likes of Min Jin Lee (Pachinko), Lauren Beukes (The Shining Girls), N. K. Jemisin (The Inheritance Trilogy), and Jeff VanderMeer (the Southern Reach series). There’s even an original six-part story from Guillermo del Toro and Chuck Hogan that Netflix is turning into a movie. Short stories are an oft-neglected form that both let you discover new authors and give established writers a space to get weird and experimental. Often, this results in some of an author’s most memorable work. Arthur C. Clarke published a lot of novels, but nothing has stuck with me quite like the haunting short The Star. But what’s also great about these series from Amazon is the freedom they offer. Historically, short stories have been available either in magazines or as part of large collections. But on a digital platform like the Kindle, you have more choice for how you engage with the stories. While I think each story in “Magic and Mystery” is worth checking out, you don’t have to buy the whole thing at once. Each short is available individually, giving the collection a sort of episodic feel. It’s like watching an anthology like Black Mirror, where as soon as one episode is done, you can decide where you want to go next, or if you want to continue at all. The stories are also cheap enough — usually running a buck or two — that they stray easily into impulse purchase territory. The drawback is that these shorts are largely exclusive to Amazon. There’s at least one exception — del Toro’s The Boy in the Iron Box is getting a physical release — but otherwise digging into these collections necessitates owning a Kindle, or reading through the app on your phone. For me at least, that’s been reason enough to keep my e-reader charged even as my shelves become stuffed with physical books.

articles.title: Spotify: música com inteligência artificial terá selo AI Persona | G1
articles.standfirst: A gigante sueca do streaming anunciou que lançará em meados de setembro o selo "AI Persona", que vai identificar criadores de conteúdo que não são pessoas reais.
articles.summary: O Spotify lançará o selo AI Persona para identificar música com inteligência artificial e garantir transparência sobre criadores que não são pessoas reais.
articles.body:
Perfil da cantora Tocanna no Spotify, artista com músicas criadas por ferramentas de IA. — Foto: Reprodução/Spotify

A gigante do streaming Spotify anunciou, nesta terça-feira (11), que lançará em meados de setembro um novo selo, chamado "AI Persona", para identificar claramente criadores de conteúdo que não são pessoas reais, mas foram gerados por inteligência artificial.

LEIA TAMBÉM: Uso de IA é comum em músicas de artistas pop nacionais, afirmam profissionais da indústria; entenda

"Os ouvintes nos disseram claramente que não gostam de ver um perfil de artista que parece humano e depois descobrir que a pessoa foi gerada por IA", afirmou a empresa em comunicado.

A medida é a iniciativa mais recente da companhia sueca para aumentar a transparência sobre como as músicas disponíveis em sua plataforma são produzidas , em meio à crescente preocupação da indústria musical com conteúdos gerados por IA.

Em abril, a empresa lançou o selo "Verificado pelo Spotify ", que indica que um perfil foi analisado e atende aos critérios de autenticidade.

"Além dos perfis de artistas que se declararem como AI Persona, também começaremos a aplicar esses selos aos perfis pertinentes", informou a empresa.

O Spotify acrescentou que perfis identificados como "AI Persona" não serão incluídos em recomendações editoriais ou personalizadas, a menos que determinado usuário siga um desses criadores fictícios.

articles.title: Amazon gets out of the MMO game
articles.summary: Amazon will be handing over live operations of the Throne and Liberty and Lost Ark MMOs in the West to other companies.
articles.body: Amazon is fully stepping back from MMOs. After saying last year that it would be halting “a significant amount” of its work on first-party AAA games, “specifically around MMOs,” Amazon will be handing over live operations of Throne and Liberty and Lost Ark in the West to other companies, according to announcements on Wednesday. Throne and Liberty will be taken over by FirstSpark Games and NC in Q4 2026. Lost Ark will be run by Smilegate starting in early 2027. When Amazon announced the broader strategy shift in October, the developers of a third MMO, New World: Aeternum, announced plans to stop offering new content updates. As of January, you can’t buy that game anymore, and it will be taken offline on January 31st, 2027. Amazon’s current gaming strategy focuses more on its Luna cloud gaming service, party games you can play on a TV with your phone (including ones with AI-powered Snoop Dogg and Arnold Schwarzenegger characters), and games that tie into other franchises Amazon is working on, like James Bond and Tomb Raider. Amazon’s gaming boss spelled it all out for me in a recent interview.

articles.title: Actor Hayden Panettiere, known for ‘Remember the Titans’ and ‘Bring It On,’ dies at 36
articles.summary: The cause and manner of death were unclear. Panettiere revealed this year that she struggled with postpartum depression and addiction, which she said led to her decision to give up custody of her daughter in 2018.
articles.body: Actor Hayden Panettiere, who was known for roles in television’s “Heroes” and “Nashville” and had recently published a memoir, has died, her father said in a statement Sunday night. She was 36. “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden,” Skip Panettiere said in a statement provided by her representative. The Greenville County Coroner’s Office said Monday that the cause of death is pending further investigation. An autopsy was completed Monday, the statement added, and “no signs of trauma were discovered that would have contributed to the death.” At around 1:50 p.m. Sunday, authorities received a 911 call about a “reported cardiac arrest” at an apartment complex, according to the coroner’s office. Police said an acquaintance of Panettiere’s made the 911 call. “Panettiere was found unresponsive inside the residence, where she had been temporarily staying,” the coroner’s office said. Advanced cardiac life support measures were initiated, but resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful, the statement added. Panettiere was pronounced dead at 2:32 p.m. “The case is under investigation by the Greenville Police Department in conjunction with the Greenville County Coroner’s Office,” police said Sunday, adding that the preliminary investigation had not indicated any signs of foul play or suspicious circumstances. Panettiere revealed this year that she previously struggled with postpartum depression and addiction, which she said led to her decision to give up custody of her only child, daughter Kaya Evdokia Klitschko, in 2018, whom she had with former partner Wladimir Klitschko, the Ukrainian professional boxer. Panettiere recently published a memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning,” which generated headlines over its revelations, including some about her past relationships. In 2024, she described the pain and grief after her younger brother, actor Jansen Panettiere, died unexpectedly of an undiagnosed heart condition the previous year. “When you lose somebody that you saw in all the important moments in your life, standing right next to you, it just rocks your world,” she told NBC’s “TODAY” show. Hayden Panettiere was born and raised in Palisades, New York, about 40 miles north of New York City, according to her Television Academy bio. Panettiere started working at 11 months old, when she appeared in television commercials, it said. She appeared on soap operas, including “One Life to Live” and “Guiding Light,” beginning at age 4. Her voice was featured as the young princess ant in “A Bug’s Life,” the animated feature, and she eventually appeared in big-screen stories, including “Remember the Titans,” “Ice Princess” and “Bring It On: All or Nothing.” One of her most impactful roles was as Juliette Barnes on television’s “Nashville.” The role earned her two Golden Globe nominations. Before that, she was Claire Bennet on the 2000s show “Heroes.” Connie Briton, Panettiere’s co-star on “Nashville,” posted several photos of the two of them together on the set with the caption: “This was Hayden. Bursting with brilliance, shining so bright. I have no words for this sad song. Just heartbreak. I love you girl. Sleep easy now. 💔” Matt Lanter, who played a boyfriend of Panettiere’s characters in both “Heroes” and ABC’s “Commander in Chief,” posted a sweet picture of her hugging him in happier times. “We always had a great time on set and tons of laughs,” Lanter wrote, saying Panettiere was “just too young” when she died. Emma Roberts, who appeared with Panettiere in the 2011 horror sequel “Scream 4,” also posted a loving photo of her kissing Panettiere on her forehead. Roberts, the niece of Julia Roberts, eulogized, “rest in peace my sweet friend,” telling the departed Panettiere that she was “so loved and you will be forever missed.” Her time shooting “Nashville” included the pressure of having had a baby and experiencing postpartum depression, she said, and at times it was too much. “That’s why I turned to substances — because the anxiety that I started having, the panic attacks that I started having,” she said in a tearful interview on the “Jay Shetty Podcast” in May. Panettiere said she always wanted to be a mother but discussed her sadness amid her postpartum depression. “I had this beautiful plan in my head, and then I had my daughter, and I knew something was just terribly, terribly wrong,” she said on the podcast. “I was miserable. I was in tears all the time. Even though the alcohol helped my nervous system calm down, it is a depressant, so over time it made things worse, not better.” Despite being apart from her daughter after she gave up custody to Klitschko, Panettiere told Shetty, she formed a strong bond with her child. “I will always want her here. I always miss her,” she said. “I always want to have my arms wrapped around her, but that’s just not the way life is right at this moment.” She continued, “I have faith that she is going to come to me and that we’re going to have an incredible relationship and bond and friendship that a lot of parents don’t get to have with their kids.” In 2018, the year “Nashville” ended its six-season run, Panettiere sold her home in the namesake city. The screen actors union SAG-AFTRA, which counted her as a member since 1994, said in a statement: “We join in mourning the sudden passing of Hayden Panettiere. Our hearts are with her daughter, family, friends and fans.” Viola Davis, who starred alongside Panettiere in the 2016 film “Custody,” paid tribute to her “amazing talent.” “I wish the world had more time with you because I had a burning curiosity about who you were becoming. I saw this beautiful Phoenix rising from the ashes. Your tests became your testimony, and your testimony became your legacy. You will be remembered,” Davis said on Instagram. Emme Rylan, who appeared with Panettiere in “Bring It On: All or Nothing,” said on Instagram: “So very sad. Rest in peace sweet soul.” Kelly Osbourne said in an Instagram Story that she was “deeply saddened by the loss of someone who meant so much to me.” “We understood each other in a way few truly can — recognizing how difficult it is to grow up in the spotlight, and how isolating it can feel even when surrounded by so many people,” Osbourne wrote, adding that Panettiere was “such a good friend to me.” Brit Shaw, who guest-starred on “Nashville,” called Panettiere’s death a “shock” on Instagram. “She had this way of making you feel at home. From the moment I walked onto the Nashville set, she made me feel like I belonged,” Shaw wrote. “We had so many good times together, and I’ll always be grateful for them.” Alyson Stoner, who succeeded Panettiere as the English voice actor for Kairi in the “Kingdom Hearts” video game franchise, also expressed her grief on Instagram. “From one Kairi to another… One sky, one destiny,” said the caption on the emotional video. “My deepest condolences to Hayden’s family, community, and the many lives Hayden reached. May you rest in freedom, Hayden.” Paul Strauss, one of Washington, D.C.’s nonvoting representatives in the U.S. Senate, shared a photo of himself with Panettiere on Instagram and said he was “devastated” by her death. “Hayden was a special person who always tried to use her platform for causes she believed in. Her advocacy to protect whales, and for DC Statehood were just some of the worthy causes she generously donated her time and energy to,” Strauss said. “A special soul gone way too soon.” Panettiere was a spokesperson for the Whaleman Foundation, an oceanic conservation group; appeared in the 2010 Oscar-winning documentary about dolphin slaughter, “The Cove”; and received the Genesis Wyler Award from the Humane Society, according to the Television Academy. “She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her— and to the millions who watched her onscreen,” her father said. articles.title: Coyote vs. Acme is even funnier because Warner Bros. Discovery tried to kill it
articles.summary: Part of what makes Coyote vs. Acme — in theaters August 28th — work so well is all the melodrama WBD whipped up.
articles.body: There’s an argument to be made that people wouldn’t be all that interested in Coyote vs. Acme if it weren’t for the way David Zaslav tried to kill it. By trying to shelve the project, Warner Bros. Discovery only drew attention to its habit of disappearing nearly completed movies in order to cash in on tax write-offs.  Coyote vs. Acme’s generally positive reviews are on the money; it really is one of the best Looney Tunes movies in years. In theory, this suggests that the movie might do well at the box office and become a case study in WBD making terrible decisions. Ironically, though, all of the drama surrounding the live-action / animated hybrid film is actually part of what makes it an enjoyable watch.  Loosely based on Ian Frazier’s Coyote v. Acme piece in The New Yorker, the new movie follows Wile E. Coyote as he concocts another harebrained scheme to kill the Road Runner. But rather than simply trying to destroy his nemesis with elaborate plans that involve various gadgets, Coyote decides to go after Acme with a lawsuit over its faulty products. Though attorney Kevin Avery (Will Forte) would rather take the settlement proposed by Acme’s legal counsel Buddy Crane (John Cena), Coyote believes he can receive a much bigger payout by going to court. And with countless examples of how Acme’s products have harmed him, Coyote’s confident that he can build a strong case. [Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kMsiD1Nky5I] Coyote vs. Acme leans into the absurd with a world in which humans and cartoon maniacs exist alongside one another. When the coyote isn’t busy trying to catch his dinner, he has to deal with all the ordinary drudgery that comes with being a productive member of society, like Avery’s niece, Paige (Lana Condor.) This and the way a bevy of Looney Tunes characters pop up as people working regular jobs brings a delightful energy to Coyote vs. Acme that’s akin to The Muppets. And by framing Acme as a cross between WBD, Apple, Tesla, and Lockheed Martin, the movie sets its story up to work as commentary about corporations screwing customers over with false promises. At its core, Coyote vs. Acme is a classic Looney Tunes project, meaning that it spends much of its runtime focusing on ridiculous gags. The movie’s script — penned by James Gunn, Jeremy Slater, and Samy Burch — features moments where Coyote and Avery grow to see one another as friends, but it’s mostly focused on showcasing how chaotic life would be in a world filled with beings who regularly defy the laws of physics with their cartoonish antics. This makes Coyote vs. Acme an excellent showcase of the way its creative team blends traditional animation with live-action footage. The movie’s set pieces are mildly amusing, but its story is so by-the-numbers that one would be hard-pressed to call it riveting. What is interesting about the film’s story is the way it makes WBD seem like a studio that’s afraid of poking fun at itself. You can almost hear Gunn, Slater, and Burch having a laugh at Zaslav’s expense as Foghorn Leghorn (Eric Bauza) is introduced as Acme’s conniving leader, and those kinds of jokes are what makes the movie feel like it might actually resonate with audiences. By going meta and not exactly trying to be a movie for children (remember, this is about a legal battle), Coyote vs. Acme highlights how WBD could be getting a bit more use out of characters like Bugs Bunny (also Bauza) and Granny (Candi Milo). Had the studio just put the movie out on its own, it might have made Zaslav and his fellow executives seem like people with an understanding of how to capitalize on legacy intellectual property. But whatever accolades Coyote vs. Acme ultimately receives will largely be attributed to Ketchup Entertainment, which bought the rights to distribute it. The box office performances for WBD’s last few Looney Tunes projects suggests that Coyote vs. Acme won’t be breaking any records before it winds up on one streaming platform or another. But when the film releases on August 28th, it will remind the public of how ready WBD was to throw it in the chipper. Especially now as the studio navigates a potential merger with Paramount, that kind of cavalier attitude toward jettisoning people’s work makes Zaslav’s WBD seem like a company that isn’t exactly committed to art. That might not matter to Zaslav, who stands to make bank regardless of whether the Paramount merger goes through. But it’s a terrible look for a studio that’s trying to maintain its reputation as one of Hollywood’s biggest players.

articles.title: Robin Williams’ Instagram account brought back to fight ‘AI abuse’
articles.summary: Robin Williams’ children are bringing back their father’s Instagram account to share his memory and combat the use of his AI likeness.
articles.body: Robin Williams’ children are taking over their father’s Instagram account after his daughter spoke out against the use of his AI likeness, as reported earlier by The Wrap. In a post on Tuesday, Zak, Zelda, and Cody Williams write that they want the late actor’s Instagram profile to be a “safe, trusted place where the stories, photos, videos, and memories shared reflect his legacy with authenticity, warmth, and care.” A story posted to Zelda Williams’ own Instagram account expands on the decision to bring back her father’s profile, saying that it’s meant to help combat “rampant AI abuse,” according to The Wrap: > I’m sorry if anyone found Dad’s old page posting again to be triggering. Believe me, I know it’s a little strange. Making that space into one where people can find authentic clips and photos of him is one of the best ways we’ve now found to fight back against rampant AI abuse of his voice and likeness on here. Robin Williams’ Instagram account remained inactive following his death in 2014. Last year, Zelda Williams asked fans to stop sending her AI-generated videos of her father. “To watch the legacies of real people be condensed down to ‘this vaguely looks and sounds like them so that’s enough’, just so other people can churn out horrible TikTok slop puppeteering them is maddening,” she wrote at the time. [Media: https://www.instagram.com/p/DcJeJG_HM3g/] Though some AI chatbots have restrictions in place to prevent users from generating images or videos with the AI likeness of a public figure or celebrity, these guardrails can still be bypassed. OpenAI’s now-shuttered Sora app became a hotbed for generating videos of copyrighted characters and celebrities, while Grok is still generating sexualized AI deepfakes of famous women, according to Wired. ByteDance’s AI model, Seedance, also struck an agreement with the Motion Picture Association after lax guardrails allowed users to generate scenes with the AI likenesses of their favorite Hollywood stars. Bad actors have even used the AI likenesses of celebrities, like Taylor Swift and Rihanna, to push scams on TikTok. Zelda, Zak, and Cody Williams add that they’re going to use their father’s Instagram account to share his “unique talent and humor with the world.”

articles.title: ‘Dune: Part Three’ sets off early ticket frenzy as fans crash sales sites
articles.summary: Fans eager to see “Dune: Part Three” on the biggest screens in December first had to survive the online ticket queue.
articles.body: Fans eager to see “Dune: Part Three” on the biggest screens in December first had to survive the online ticket queue. Many on social media reported long waits and ticketing site crashes Tuesday as they scrambled to snag seats for early IMAX 70 mm screenings in December. “Am I tripping or did every website for Dune 3 IMAX 70MM crash?” an X user wrote. “Help! Has anybody beaten this bug/error to secure Dune 3 tickets???” another person asked, sharing a screenshot of the Fandango site with a message that read: “Internal server error. Please try again.” “I HAVE THREE DEVICES OPEN TRYING TO GET DUNE TICKETS AND NONE OF THEM WORK,” another X user said. The rollout is the latest sign of a growing frenzy around seeing major movies in specific premium formats, in which securing the right seat and screen has become an event of its own. A similar rush unfolded in June, when advance sales for Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” overwhelmed AMC’s website, with some moviegoers reporting hourslong waits. “Dune: Part Three” is the latest installment in Warner Bros. Pictures’ adaptation of Frank Herbert’s seminal 1965 novel set thousands of years in the future in a world devastated by ecological collapse. The movie, directed by Denis Villeneuve, picks up 17 years after the previous one, with Paul Atreides (played by Timothée Chalamet) ruling the galaxy while in a political marriage to Princess Irulan (Florence Pugh). The sci-fi franchise, which also stars Zendaya and Jason Momoa, has become an audience must-see since the first installment’s box-office success in 2021. Though the new film isn’t being released until Dec. 18, some fans had already bragged about getting their tickets in April when IMAX first released a limited number of tickets for some screenings. Last week, IMAX sent out an email telling fans to “Save the Date” for another chance to get early tickets. “Dear IMAX fans, You showed up in a big way when the first DUNE: PART THREE tickets were released,” the email read. “We’ve heard you and know you want more access to tickets and more time to plan. So, here you go... The next opportunity to get DUNE: PART THREE tickets will arrive in one week on Tuesday, August 18 at 9:00 a.m. PST. This ticket drop will unlock more opening week DUNE Insider Screenings in IMAX and IMAX 70mm, so mark your calendars, make your plans, and get ready to return to Arrakis.” By Tuesday, people’s efforts to secure tickets had turned into viral mayhem. Fans reported that at certain points, AMC’s and Fandango’s apps had crashed. (AMC and Fandango did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday.) Several people who managed to get tickets said it took them over an hour of waiting. A person on X posted a picture of a line wrapped around an AMC in New York, where fans tried to secure tickets in person. Some people also began reselling their early tickets on eBay for up to $1,000. The demand for multiformat viewing experiences is fueling moviegoing FOMO, reshaping how studios market tentpole films and prompting an effort to bring order to an increasingly crowded premium-screen landscape. Some frustrated cinephiles argue theater chains and studios should do more to ensure a smoother ticketing process. “If you’re going to turn movie ticket-buying into a competitive sport, then you need to have the tech and UX to support that shift,” film critic Barry Hertz wrote on X. “Theatrical exhibition is not easy, certainly, but it doesn’t need to be this hard.” AMC CEO Adam Aron addressed fan frustration Tuesday on X. He said that “ticketing traffic across AMC’s website and mobile app reached levels approximately three times higher than what we experienced during the Spider-Man: Brand New Day ticket launch, which itself followed strong advance sales for The Odyssey ticket launch before that.” “It’s not that our systems totally failed,” he added. “We have been selling enormous numbers of tickets today, but when any of our customers experience less than our best, it is just not right.” Aron wrote that while there was “much discussion internally” and preparation for the ticket launch, “We thought we were ready, but we weren’t.” The theater chain, Aron said, requires “about $2 million of IT programming resource” to “fully address the issue.” “Of course, that money has been approved already,” he wrote, “and we’ve asked our IT team to move at a whirlwind speed to take whatever steps are needed so that our ticketing systems are — in all situations and in all quantities —again top shelf.”

articles.title: Amazon seemingly leaked Jason Statham’s entire Mutiny movie
articles.summary: The film isn’t supposed to hit theaters for two days, but it was briefly available to stream on Prime Video.
articles.body: Jason Statham’s upcoming film Mutiny is set to hit theaters on August 21st, but for at least an hour today it was available to stream in full on the US version of Amazon Prime Video. My colleague Dominic Preston was able to verify that all 1 hour and 35 minutes of the movie was available to watch on Amazon’s streaming platform, though it now shows as “unavailable.” The Mutiny website and marketing materials state that it’ll only be available in theaters when it’s officially released in two days. There’s nothing to suggest that this was released on Prime Video intentionally, or that it’s intended to be some marketing stunt — neither the Punch Palace Productions and MadRiver Pictures production studios, nor US distributor Lionsgate, are owned by Amazon. We have reached out to Amazon for comment. It’s unclear when Mutiny was added to Prime Video US. The Prime Video listing is fully populated with the cast list, video thumbnail, and a blurb that reads: “After his billionaire industrialist boss is murdered in front of him, Cole Reed is set up to take the fall for the crime — leaving him on the run as he works to uncover a conspiracy.” [Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FKSdXH89jbo&list=PLJ7A97yl9oXphnKstrll_GetLGHMNodCn&index=1] Update, August 19th: The film is no longer available to stream.

articles.title: We played The Duskbloods, the Switch 2’s wildest new exclusive
articles.summary: The Duskbloods is the latest game from Elden Ring developer FromSoftware, and it’s launching exclusively on the Switch 2 in 2026.
articles.body: The Duskbloods is a world away from the approachable games Nintendo is known for. But for its next Switch 2 exclusive, the company has partnered with Elden Ring developer FromSoftware on a hardcore multiplayer game about vampires. And after spending a few hours playing through its gothic world at FromSoft’s offices in Tokyo, I’m convinced that The Duskbloods could end up being one of the most important exclusives for Nintendo’s latest console. It’s a notable change for the company. People buy Nintendo consoles for Nintendo games. That’s a generally accepted truth, and also one that’s backed up by data — a quick glance at the bestselling games across platforms like the Switch and Nintendo 3DS reveals expected names like Mario Kart, Pokémon, and Animal Crossing. Titles from outside developers can be an integral part of broadening a platform’s appeal, but that’s something that Nintendo has historically struggled with. Which is what makes The Duskbloods so intriguing. The Duskbloods is not an easy game to describe. In a universe of vampires that spans multiple time periods, eight players, controlling vampiric characters known as the Bloodsworn, descend on a level filled with enemies and gigantic boss creatures. Over the course of several phases the group is whittled down until only a few remain, who must then fight until only one is left. This isn’t a Fortnite-style battle royale, however. Instead, The Duskbloods is designed to mix the thrill of competitive play with the roleplaying fantasy that FromSoft has become known for through games like Dark Souls and Bloodborne. --- [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/The_Duskbloods_12.png?quality=90&strip=all] Read next: FromSoftware can do anything --- Key to this is something that the game calls “virtue.” Essentially, it’s a system that allows you accumulate points over the course of a match by doing just about everything. You can get virtue by collecting the most items, or by killing the most minor enemies, or by taking down boss creatures like a gigantic frog with far too many humanlike teeth. There are virtue points for exploration — the levels are littered with hidden corpses you can discover — and in the later rounds you can get a huge burst of virtue points by defeating other players on specific points of the map, or making a pledge at an altar before another player stops you. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/The_Duskbloods_17.png?quality=90&strip=all] Each match is divided into four phases, and the player count slowly shrinks through what’s known as “the culling.” Basically, if you don’t have enough virtue points by the time a round ends then you’re out. How many points you need depends entirely on how much virtue other players have collected. The idea is that, even if you maybe aren’t the best one-on-one fighter, you can still progress through the game and make it to the final phase, since there are so many different ways to earn points. And aside from the final round, you’ll respawn immediately after dying with your virtue intact, which makes it easier to try things and explore without fear of the game ending. In practice, The Duskbloods can be an overwhelming experience, at least initially. It took me some time to wrap my head around the points system; in most competitive multiplayer games, killing other players is the clearest path to victory. Here, though, that’s not the case, particularly at the beginning. Instead, the early rounds are best spent exploring the map, defeating weaker enemies, and generally strengthening your character by acquiring items and experience. And there’s a lot more to The Duskbloods’ complexity than just the points system. For starters, there are multiple vampiric characters to play as, each of whom has a very different playstyle. In the early version of the game I played — which is the same as the network test that will run later in August — there are six characters to choose from. There’s an aging senator who wields a rapier that doubles as a cane, and who can both summon a prehistoric bird as a ranged attack and temporarily transform into a bloodthirsty dinosaur. There’s a ninja with circular blades, a mysterious man who can shoot columns of fire from a stone embedded in his hand, and an armor-clad weirdo named Zork who carries around an electrified chunk of undersea cable. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/The_Duskbloods_19.png?quality=90&strip=all] Each character plays differently — some are quick and nimble, others lumbering yet powerful — with their own distinct abilities. During each game you can also find and summon companion characters, called kin, which lend help in battle and can also be leveled up over the course of a match. These can be everything from sword-wielding samurai to gigantic wolves. My favorite was a soprano who was also a wrestler, suplexing enemies while singing a song that helped improve my defensive capabilities. You can also turn certain enemies into your minions by sucking their blood and exerting your influence over them. There are random events that can happen — a zeppelin that barrages the level with bombs, a lightning storm that zaps players to random points on the map — as well as “sigils” you can equip that give you a specific and sometimes strange task to perform that can earn you lots of virtue. For instance, a sigil might be based on revenge, and task you with finding a specific player and killing them. Or it might ask you to find the other player who is your character’s lost love and… propose to them in the middle of the match. These are designed to give you both an additional way to earn points in a match and a role to play in the story. I should note that what I played is missing some key features that will be in the final game, most notably the majority of the character customization and story elements, which will be a major part of the appeal for existing FromSoft fans. Similarly, while all of the games I played ended in a fight to the death, there will be other possible win conditions, like the last group of players teaming up to defeat a boss. And all of that is just scratching the surface. There is a lot going on in The Duskbloods. After spending several hours playing the game with other members of the press over the course of two days, I felt like I had just begun to grasp how everything worked. That’s a far cry from the pick-up-and-play nature that has made Nintendo’s online games like Splatoon and Mario Kart such major successes. Those are games that are easy to grasp from the moment you pick up the controller. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/The_Duskbloods_15.png?quality=90&strip=all] But at the same time, The Duskbloods has the potential to do something very significant. With Elden Ring, FromSoft took an extremely intimidating genre of action RPG and opened it up to a new audience by fusing that style of game onto an open world that gave players more choice for how they approached challenges. The result was a massive hit: Elden Ring has sold more than 30 million copies, its expansion Shadow of the Erdtree sold 10 million, and the game is being made into a Hollywood movie. The Duskbloods, meanwhile, is tackling the similarly intimidating field of competitive multiplayer. And while The Duskbloods is still pretty hardcore, it’s designed in a way that attempts to give players things to do even if they can’t win a match. The live-service space may be a disaster right now, but online multiplayer games still make up the bulk of time people spend playing games. And the combination of online play and FromSoft’s renowned fantasy worldbuilding could eventually lure a new type of player to the Switch 2, at a time when dedicated video game platforms are largely struggling. There’s a lot of risk inherent to a game like this. Control developer Remedy Entertainment, for instance, tried something similar with the co-op shooter FBC: Firebreak, and that didn’t end so well. The Duskbloods has the added challenge of launching exclusively on the Switch 2, a platform that’s not yet known for these kinds of multiplayer experiences. But the same things that make the game a risk are also what make it so fascinating. The Duskbloods is unlike anything else in the Switch 2’s lineup — and it could help Nintendo reach players beyond Zelda and Mario fans.

articles.title: FromSoftware can do anything
articles.summary: Elden Ring studio FromSoftware is going down a different path with The Duskbloods, a multiplayer game that’s exclusive to the Nintendo Switch 2.
articles.body: There’s something just a little bit different about FromSoftware’s office in Tokyo. Like with any other successful video game studio, there’s extensive security to get in the door, a minimalist lobby with framed posters from the studio’s most recent releases, and a large glass display case filled with statues from ceremonies ranging from the BAFTAs to The Game Awards. But the hallways are painted black, a fitting theme for a developer known for crafting dark, gothic worlds and a hint at what new creations are lurking inside. While it has largely become known for a singular style of action game — dubbed “Soulslike,” after the massively influential Dark Souls series — FromSoft has steadily continued to try new things, pushing its signature style into new genres. Perhaps the most extreme example of this is the studio’s next release: The Duskbloods, a competitive multiplayer game set in a world of vampires that will be exclusive to the Switch 2 and published by Nintendo when it launches later this year. It’s a new genre, new setting, new platform, and new publisher all rolled into one game. But after Elden Ring, which has sold more than 30 million copies since it launched in 2022, the team at FromSoft now also feels more assured in expanding their horizons. “With the success of Elden Ring, as a company it has definitely allowed us to explore, I wouldn’t say risky ideas, but things that we might not have had the confidence for,” FromSoftware president Hidetaka Miyazaki, who also directed both Elden Ring and The Duskbloods, told me during a recent hands-on event at the studio’s office. [Image: Hidetaka Miyazaki. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Mr.-Miyazaki-Headshot_Vertical-copy.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The studio’s rise to this point has been slow and steady. FromSoft’s first release was the dungeon crawling RPG King’s Field in 1994, and while it launched a consistent stream of titles after that — including the cult-hit mech battling Armored Core series — it was more than a decade later when the studio really started making its mark with the release of Demon’s Souls in 2009. Directed by Miyazaki, the game thrust players into a harsh fantasy world, one where death was a constant and the combat was punishing. It was an experience that demanded a lot from players, but also rewarded their patience with thrilling victories and a story that gradually revealed itself. It was an unlikely hit that spawned a new genre of action games, and was followed up by a number of successors, including a trilogy of Dark Souls titles and the Victorian-era-inspired Bloodborne in 2015. Those games were all successes, selling millions of copies, but it wasn’t until Elden Ring that the studio had its first blockbuster hit. The game not only sold well, but spawned a large-scale expansion, a co-op spinoff called Nightreign, and an upcoming film adaptation from A24 and director Alex Garland. Part of what made Elden Ring a hit was that it took what FromSoft had become known for — relentless action, subtle storytelling, and immersive worlds — and translated it into an open-world adventure and gave players more freedom to explore its bleak and beautiful fantastical realm. Even with its signature game style cemented, FromSoft was continuously experimenting. Sandwiched in between the launches of Dark Souls 3 (2016) and Elden Ring (2022) were a pair of one-off games — a solemn VR story called Déraciné in 2018, and a ninja action game called Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice a year later — that showed the studio expanding its range. At the time, Miyazaki, who directed both games, explained FromSoft’s approach to taking on new projects. “I think one of the studio’s characteristics is to embrace wholeheartedly what we feel is interesting; what we perceive to be worthwhile, cool, or beautiful; and to place these ideals at the foundation of the games we make,” he told me in 2019. “Part of those things we feel may deviate slightly from what is considered to have mass appeal. This ‘unorthodox’ nature could well be what ties our games and our culture together.” [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/The_Duskbloods_16.png?quality=90&strip=all] The Duskbloods may seem like a big departure, but it also fits neatly into this philosophy. Over the years, FromSoft had steadily been injecting multiplayer elements into its largely single-player games; in Elden Ring, for instance, you can summon other players to help you in battle. As the studio experimented in this realm, a number of multiplayer-centric ideas were filed away. “There are a lot of ideas that we had wanted to try that didn’t necessarily fit in that context of a single-player game,” Miyazaki said during the Duskbloods preview in Tokyo. “Those pile up over the years.” That eventually culminated into The Duskbloods. Development on The Duskbloods began in 2021 and originated on the first Switch before eventually migrating to its successor. The game consists of matches where eight players, each controlling a vampiric fighter, have to both fight against the monsters prowling the level as well as compete with each other. The combat is faster than a traditional FromSoft game, and the exploration is much more vertical — you can triple-jump your way up large towers — but it also has many of the studio’s telltale characteristics, from its dark, haunting world to the fact that players will die repeatedly. (For more on how The Duskbloods plays, check out my hands-on right here.) But all of those new elements also made the development process difficult, and Miyazaki says that working with Nintendo has been extremely helpful in this regard. “The Duskbloods is a challenging game for us,” he says. “There are a lot of new things in terms of designing the systems and the rules, and it requires a lot of fine-tuning and adjustments, and Nintendo has provided a lot of support in that regard. Things like onboarding and tutorials for players are something that we are historically not great at, so the support they’ve provided in that regard has been very, very good and we think that it’s been a great relationship in that sense.” On a technical level, Miyazaki notes that the team initially struggled with getting The Duskbloods to work on Nintendo’s previous console, so the reveal of the Switch 2 came as something of a relief. “We were definitely very happy when we heard about the Switch 2, because we were thinking, ‘How are we going to do this?’” Miyazaki says. “The Switch 2 came along and all of those problems were solved.” The game is being designed in part to appeal to players who might not traditionally be interested in competitive multiplayer, a genre that can be intimidating to a lot of people. While The Duskbloods does involve fighting against other players, it also gives them other things to do, whether it’s killing minor enemies to gain experience or exploring the landscape in search of helpful items or sidekicks that can aid in battle. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/The_Duskbloods_18.png?quality=90&strip=all] “We really just want as many players to enjoy our games as possible,” Miyazaki says. “Not just having it be solely [player vs. player], but having more indirect ways that you can compete in the match and enjoy it, is definitely something that we wanted to implement to accommodate players. From a role-playing and story aspect as well, we didn’t want it to be something where you had to always win every single match to enjoy the game. We wanted you to be able to unlock aspects of the story and enjoy it at your own pace, even if you’re not necessarily doing great in every match. And if [players] go in wanting to know more about the story and that’s what interests them, that’s great. And as they reveal that and play more of the game, they might find that they do like the PvP more than they thought. We’re hoping that is an entryway.” It might look like a shift in strategy, particularly as the studio’s last two releases have both focused on multiplayer play. But The Duskbloods is actually an extension of how the studio has worked for years: a big departure that builds off of the developer’s previous work in natural ways. It’s still set in a dark fantasy world, it still stars a cast of eclectic weirdos, and it still thrusts players into a space where they have to master complex systems in order to survive. It just puts these ideas in a new, multiplayer-specific context. Because of this, Miyazaki says that The Duskbloods doesn’t necessarily represent any kind of change in how the studio operates. FromSoft has always made whatever it wanted, and Elden Ring’s success has only made it bolder. “We’re not super rigid,” he says. “It’s more just, if we find something that we want to make and we think it’s a great idea, we’ll make it.”

articles.title: El actor Ray MacDonald muere a los 49 años tras sufrir un infarto mientras dormía en su domicilio en Bangkok
articles.standfirst: El trágico suceso ocurrió durante la madrugada del miércoles 19 de agosto
articles.summary: El trágico suceso ocurrió durante la madrugada del miércoles 19 de agosto
articles.body: El actor británico-tailandés Ray MacDonald ha fallecido a los 49 años tras sufrir un infarto agudo de miocardio mientras dormía en su domicilio ubicado en el área residencial de Phatthanakan, en Bangkok. El trágico suceso ocurrió durante la madrugada del miércoles 19 de agosto y su entorno familiar señaló que el artista acumulaba una fatiga extrema debido a un exigente e intenso ritmo de trabajo. Su esposa, Sarinya ‘Mam’, lo encontró inconsciente en el sofá del salón frente al televisor a primera hora de la mañana, cuando se disponía a despertarlo para acompañar a su hijo pequeño en su primer día de colegio. Al principio, pensó que simplemente seguía dormido, pero rápidamente se dio cuenta de que algo no iba bien. Los servicios de emergencia acudieron rápidamente a la vivienda y le practicaron maniobras de reanimación cardiopulmonar durante varios minutos, pero no pudieron hacer nada por salvar su vida. Su amigo cercano, el también actor Chakrit Yamnam, explicó a medios locales que MacDonald padecía obstrucciones graves en varias arterias coronarias. Esto interrumpió el flujo sanguíneo de su corazón y provocó la muerte mientras descansaba. Nacido en mayo de 1977 y de ascendencia escocesa, el también presentador y modelo comenzó su andadura pública en el fútbol juvenil antes de ganar una beca en el Reino Unido y regresar a Tailandia como modelo publicitario. Fue en los años 90 cuando saltó a la fama absoluta en la televisión tailandesa como presentador del exitoso programa juvenil ‘Teen Talk’. Ganó el Premio Nacional de Cine Suphannahong al Mejor Actor en dos años consecutivos, en 1997 y 1998, por sus papeles en ‘Fun Bar Karaoke’ y ‘Love: Designate’. En los últimos años se había alejado de las pantallas para centrarse en los contenidos de viajes de su canal de YouTube, ‘Rayro’, donde acumulaba miles de seguidores.

articles.title: Her name is Chanty Beluga. And she’s all over your social media feed.
articles.summary: Whether she’s ordering takeout or introducing herself at a pool party, she’s going to make sure you know her name.
articles.body: She’s going to a restaurant. She’s ordering takeout. She’s getting in an Uber. In every instance, she makes sure to drop her name: Chanty Beluga. Who is this smiling, millennial blond woman whose videos have gone viral on TikTok? And where did that hypnotic and unique name come from? The character is the alter ego of comedian and actor Courtney O’Donnell, who posts TikTok videos of herself as Chanty Beluga. Cheerful and demurely dressed, Chanty Beluga is always finding herself in situations where she has to use her goofy name. She’s checking in at a restaurant, ordering takeout and introducing herself at a pool party. The videos are quick and simple. Just a woman casually saying her ridiculous name, which seems to roll off the tongue and promote repeat listening. The character has already spawned multiple fan accounts on TikTok. “This is so dumb and I see myself becoming rapidly obsessed with it,” one follower commented on a TikTok video of Chanty at a coffee shop. “No notes. Just a woman named Chanty Beluga in situations where she makes her name known.” “Classic Chanty,” another one wrote. “I would die for Chanty Beluga,” another commented. O’Donnell is a Los Angeles-based comedian who has a separate TikTok account under her real name. She posts short comedy skits as different, non-Chanty Beluga characters, from the host of the fictional “Yup, She Went There” podcast to a divorcée singing through the heartbreak. She posted her first Chanty Beluga video on July 28 introducing herself, and it was a hit with nearly 500,000 views. O’Donnell told Rolling Stone that she came up with the catchy name in the middle of the night while filming the upcoming comedy “Stephanie, Bride to Be” in Brooklyn, New York. She and the cast were “being silly” when it popped into her head. “And I said, ‘Hi, my name’s Chanty,’ and we thought that was funny,” she said. “I was like, ‘Actually, my name is Chanty Beluga.’ We said the full name, and it seriously went viral in the room. We just could not stop saying Chanty Beluga.” The Chanty Beluga skits are so short that they allow O’Donnell’s followers to have fun by building out a longer story for the character. “Chanty doesn’t play abt her takeout,” one follower commented on a video of Chanty Beluga ordering food. The blank canvas of a character who’s not much beyond a funny name allows the internet to take it and run with it. “She’s a Barbie doll. She’s a paper doll. You can put her in any situation. She can do anything,” O’Donnell told Rolling Stone. “I had this instinct to really build her up and create this crazy backstory, but I thought it was more interesting to allow the internet to create its own.” Count Major League Baseball among those followers. The MLB X account posted on Aug. 18 that a woman named “Chanty Beluga” was presenting that day’s schedule of baseball games. “Sometimes you go viral for something that you didn’t connect to, and I actually think this is really fun,” O’Donnell told USA Today. “I love pretending to be this woman on the internet who’s sort of quirky and basic and talking to people in the comments like I’m her.” Then there’s one simple reason. Saying “Chanty Beluga” is fun. “Something about the intonation of the words that feels like crack to say,” O’Donnell told Rolling Stone. Now the question is whether Chanty Beluga will reach the internet heights of 6-7 before people inevitably have had enough. “I like the idea that she is the 6-7 for the girls and the gays,” O’Donnell told USA Today. “That would be really amazing. I don’t know. We’ll have to see. I’d be very happy. These things have a short shelf life, so I’m happy to just kind of be a part of it for now and let people have their fun. If we see some Halloween costumes, I won’t be mad.”

articles.title: Why soccer fans are sliding into Olivia Rodrigo's Instagram comments
articles.summary: The pop star’s account has been infiltrated by fans of FC Barcelona after the signing of Rodri, a Spanish midfielder who has publicly shunned social media.
articles.body:
Two weeks ago, Olivia Rodrigo posted photos to Instagram of herself at Lollapalooza in Chicago, where she joined the Smashing Pumpkins for a surprise performance of "Thirty-Three."

In one shot, she appeared to be backstage holding a cup of tea. In the other, she was onstage alongside frontman Billy Corgan.

"Olivia + Smashing Pumpkins was the crossover I never knew I needed," one fan wrote in the comments section.

"My favorite band and my favorite modern pop artist in one," wrote another.

But the comments about the unlikely collaboration were soon infiltrated by fans of FC Barcelona, which earlier this week announced the signing of Rodri, a Spanish midfielder and winner of the 2026 World Cup Golden Ball as the best player in this year's final.

"Welcome to Barça Rodri 💙♥️" one commenter wrote.

"I know you are not Rodri, but welcome to Barca anyways," wrote another.

So why are Barça fans using Rodrigo's Instagram account to welcome Rodri (full name: Rodrigo Hernández Cascante) to the team?

There are a few reasons. Rodri, who most recently played for Manchester City, doesn't have a public Instagram account, which was evident in 2024, when he won the Ballon d'Or for best soccer player.

Real Madrid fans who were upset that Rodri won the award — and not Vinícius Júnior — also flooded Rodrigo's Instagram account, saying he was undeserving of the annual honor. (As Marca reports , Argentine soccer player Rodrigo De Paul was also sent comments intended for his similarly named peer.)

Real Madrid fans are abusing Olivia Rodrigo on Instagram thinking that she is Rodri 😭 pic.twitter.com/aKcrPwbM0Y — Footy Humour (@FootyHumour) October 29, 2024

Real Madrid fans are abusing Olivia Rodrigo on Instagram thinking that she is Rodri 😭 pic.twitter.com/aKcrPwbM0Y

— Footy Humour (@FootyHumour) October 29, 2024

Some commenters say the new round of Barça-related comments has less to do with mistaken identity and more about riffing on the 2024 Real Madrid hijinks.

While she's not, in fact, Rodri, Rodrigo does have ties to FC Barcelona.

Culers, Olivia Rodrigo has a message for you! 💬 @spotify @oliviarodrigo 🩷 pic.twitter.com/WFrqUG8ppB — FC Barcelona (@FCBarcelona) May 10, 2026

Culers, Olivia Rodrigo has a message for you! 💬 @spotify @oliviarodrigo 🩷 pic.twitter.com/WFrqUG8ppB

— FC Barcelona (@FCBarcelona) May 10, 2026

The club released a special limited-edition jersey with Rodrigo's initials last season as part of a sponsorship with Spotify.

And earlier this year, she wished Barcelona luck ahead of its rival match, El Clásico, against Real Madrid — which Rodrigo attended .

articles.body:
Welcome to Trust Me, I Watch Everything , a weekly guide to all the new movies out each Friday.

This week's buzziest release is the sixth entry in the Insidious horror franchise, Insidious: Out of the Further, which takes things in an exciting new direction. The latest film from Jane Schoenbrun, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, also expands nationwide, as does the Anthony Bourdain biopic Tony and Matthew McConaughey's outstanding The Rivals of Amziah King .

If you'd rather stay home, you can now rent or buy Toy Story 5, one of the biggest box-office hits of the year.

Want to stick to a streaming service you're likely already paying for? Steven Soderbergh's The Christophers is well worth a watch on Hulu, and the jump-scare fest Passenger makes its way to Paramount+.

Movies newly available on streaming services you may already have

The biggest release : Insidious: Out of the Further

Why I liked it: Insidious: Out of the Further has to be one of the most inspired sixth entries in a franchise that I can think of, especially when you consider that it likely only exists because 2023's Insidious: The Red Door was such a hit, despite being the weakest entry.

That film closed the, uh, red door on the Lambert family's story, so in Out of the Further, we're introduced to a new family and a bevy of spooky new ghouls. Gemma, a young mother raising her daughter in the house she grew up in, discovers that not only can she travel into the Further, but she also possesses a very special ability: She can bring what lives in the Further back to the real world. It's a fun, goofy twist that brings a whole new dimension to the proceedings (pun intended).

Despite ultimately functioning as a metaphor for trauma — a modern horror trope so prevalent it's barely worth mentioning at this point, just assume it's the case — the movie works because it's both scary and silly. The jump scares are incredibly effective, and the entities from the Further are unsettling and/or gross to varying degrees. It's so earnestly committed to the movie's world and its random rules that it's easy to get wrapped up in it all.

The horror set pieces are truly excellent, including a standout sequence involving a pillow fort and endless couch cushions that brings Backrooms to mind, and another one involving the grossest visit to the dentist you'll likely ever experience. (Hopefully, at least.)

It leans into the ridiculousness in the back half in a way that may lose some audience members, but really won me over. It's visually inventive throughout, especially when the characters jump back and forth between the Further and reality. The childhood trauma stuff, despite earning a perfunctory eye roll from me up top, is actually well-established and unexpectedly satisfying on a narrative level by the end. They earned it!

It's still so fun that scream queen Lin Shaye, 82, is a genuine movie star, and she's well-deployed here, tethering this entry to the others in a fun way. Also, her annoying sidekicks are nowhere to be found, which is a plus, as far as I'm concerned.

Insidious: Out of the Further is a successful standalone entry in this long-running franchise. The most exciting part may be that the creatives involved here seem to have figured out how to keep things fresh moving forward. I hope it's not long before we get Insidious: Back to the Further.

What other critics are saying : Reviews are split pretty much right down the middle. TheWrap's Amelia Emberwing writes that it "overcomes a barely OK screenplay to be a fun (disgusting, sometimes terrifying and occasionally funny) ride with a good heart." Johnny Oleksinski at the New York Post wasn't a fan, writing, "Raw thrills, visual or psychological, would be fine if they didn't come alongside so many gobbledygook explainers. Trying to pump logic into this is foolish and tiresome."

How to watch : Insidious: Out of the Further is now playing in theaters nationwide .

Another option: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma

Why I liked it: Jane Schoenbrun's follow-up to the extremely personal I Saw the TV Glow is arguably even more personal, exploring an extremely specific feeling while saying so much about horror movies, sexuality, identity, shame and the intersection of all these things that it doesn't matter if you don't personally connect to every single element. Unlike its predecessor, which is deeply moving but also fairly humorless, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma is laugh-out-loud funny and joyful. It couldn't be further in tone from TV Glow despite exploring similar ideas. It's fun !

Both films are about movies, specifically examining how people discover more about themselves through the media they consume. We are what we eat, cinema-wise, so to speak. In Camp Miasma, Hacks star Hannah Einbinder plays a queer director making a slasher franchise sequel who becomes obsessed with casting the original film's "final girl" — played by X-Files legend Gillian Anderson in full Sunset Boulevard Norma Desmond mode — leading both women into psychological and sexual chaos.

It's easy to draw a line between the lead character, a Sundance wunderkind queer filmmaker, and Schoenbrun, who has likely been on the receiving end of offers similar to the one depicted in the movie. Einbinder gives a stunningly confident star-making turn here, and Anderson is having a ball with her Southern-fried nonchalance.

The movie cleverly connects the idea of a sexual awakening with the plot of a slasher film in which a masked killer, literally named Little Death — aka le petit mort, famously a French idiom for an orgasm — must be awakened from a deep slumber from a hole in the bottom of the lake before they go on a blood-soaked killing spree.

The film is at its most interesting when it explores the fake Camp Miasma franchise, clearly modeled after the Friday the 13th series but also drawing inspiration from other genre classics, including Sleepaway Camp and its problematic reveal . The opening credit sequence detailing Miasma 's trajectory over the years is an assured bit of filmmaking and a smart way to deliver exposition. There's an unforgettable kill sequence scored to the last song you'd ever expect, and that anachronism inspires questions of how well we actually remember the content of the movies we love, and how much is tied up in nostalgia.

Both Camp Miasma and TV Glow don't exactly require the context that filmmaker Jane Schoenbrun is transgender and had recently transitioned prior to making the latter film — there's a lot more to explore in both works than just gender identity. But with that knowledge, both films open up and become deeply moving treatises on accepting yourself for who you really are and the benefits that come with it. The ultimate message of TV Glow is that if you've never felt comfortable in your own body, there is still time to figure that out and live a full, happy life once you've had that moment of self-enlightenment. In Camp Miasma, a character who has always disassociated during sex and never enjoyed it learns how to get out of their own head and enjoy the moment — with the help of the movies, of course.

Divorced from any gendered reading, I Saw the TV Glow is about the transformative power of watching art, especially art you're too young to fully understand, and how it's often the first place kids can see themselves in a truly deep and meaningful way. Before we figure out our own identities, the movies and TV shows we watch help us get there. Camp Miasma can best be summed up by a line of dialogue from the movie: "I think I saw too many movies as a kid, and it f****d me up real bad."

What other critics are saying: It's very well-reviewed. Rolling Stone's David Fear writes, "It goes beyond being a paean to trash fandom, and transforms into something much deeper and grander. They have made their Miasma -sterpiece." The AP's Lindsay Bahr dubs it "a thoughtfully constructed fever dream that wears its high and low brow references on its sleeve."

How to watch: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma is now playing in theaters nationwide .

Mutiny: Jason Statham's latest Jason Statham movie delivers exactly what you'd expect from it, and not an ounce more. After witnessing his billionaire boss's murder and being framed for the crime, Cole Reed (Statham) boards a cargo ship on a one-man crusade to avenge the death, only to discover an international human trafficking conspiracy. It's about as boilerplate as it gets and plays more like a straight-to-video variant of this type of thing, though it does come alive in the action scenes. Unfortunately, there aren't quite enough of those sequences for this to rank in the top tier of Statham joints. They're selling it as " Die Hard on a boat" as if Steven Seagal didn't already do that way back in 1992! Get tickets .

It Ends: I never connected with this surreal, minimalist, no-budget indie, an alleged thriller about a group of recent college graduates who get stuck on a road that simply won't end. The entire thing is meant to be taken as a metaphor for life itself — more specifically, about the existential dread people of that age might face nowadays amid the pandemic, A.I. and other developments that might make the transition from childhood to adulthood fraught and the future uncertain. There may be enough meat on the bone for an episode of The Twilight Zone, but it bored me at feature length. Maybe if it engaged with the supernatural horrors on the periphery instead of going all-in on its central metaphor, it would've been more fun. Your mileage may vary! Get tickets .

The Rivals of Amziah King : This genre-bending indie gem, starring Matthew McConaughey, is wholly unique and incredibly charming, with a few moments of genuine "movies don't get any better than this" transcendence. McConaughey is excellent — the best he's been in ages and maybe ever. Read my full review here as the movie expands to a nationwide release. Get tickets .

Tony : Canadian filmmaker Matt Johnson ( Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie, Blackberry) leaps into the mainstream with Tony, a melancholy yet always charming coming-of-age dramedy. It also happens to be a biopic about Anthony Bourdain, covering a very specific chapter of the late chef's early days, loosely adapted from his breakthrough book, Kitchen Confidential . Read my full review here as the movie expands to a nationwide release. Get tickets .

Why I liked it: Toy Story 5 continues the storied franchise's tradition of laughs, tears and, frankly, just being damn good movies that both kids and adults can enjoy.

When Bonnie receives a Lilypad tablet as a gift and becomes obsessed, Buzz, Woody, Jessie and the rest of the gang have to go head-to-head with the all-new threat to playtime.

What's most impressive here is the way the movie understands the multi-pronged threat that technology poses to children: how it changes the very nature of "play" to the point where playing with toys is discouraged, and why using a tablet to communicate with your classmates as the only way to connect, especially for shy kids, can be a big disadvantage.

It took becoming a parent for me to realize that every single one of these movies is, quite obviously, about parenting. In case that wasn't made clear enough, there's a shot toward the end of the film that makes it fact, with Bonnie's parents and Buzz and Woody positioned so we're watching both sets of "parents" react.

It may not reach the highs of the original trilogy, but it has a renewed sense of purpose that wasn't quite present in the fourth entry. By focusing on the very real threats children face from our societal push toward "smart" toys and the proliferation of iPads and tablets, Toy Story 5 more than justifies its existence, even if the messaging stops short of going full "analog is better, and tech is inherently bad for children's development." Reminding children that nothing can replace face-to-face contact, and that simply hanging out, playing and using your imagination is the best way to form community, is an important lesson, particularly relevant today. But there is some cognitive dissonance required when the movie tries to have its cake and eat it too about tech's invasion into our lives — they have to sell Lilypad, after all.

What other critics are saying: It's getting mostly positive reviews! Nick Schager at the Daily Beast writes: "A cute and funny sequel that treads well-worn territory and yet manages to elicit its fair share of waterworks, it's not the series' best but, in most respects, is still better than the rest." TheWrap's William Bibbiani , meanwhile, calls it "enjoyable but repetitive."

How to watch: Toy Story 5 is now available to rent or buy on Apple TV , Prime Video and other VOD platforms.

📺 Movies newly available on streaming services you may already have

Why I liked it: Steven Soderbergh's latest film sees the prolific filmmaker dropping all pretense and making the "it's about making art!" element the text instead of the subtext. In the film, the estranged children of a once-famous artist (Ian McKellen) hire a forger (Michaela Coel) to complete his unfinished works so they can be "discovered" and sold after his death.

It's a moving examination of the aging artist: what inspires you and what stops you from seeing it through, as well as the meaning hidden in the work that maybe even the artist wasn't cognizant of but is absolutely there.

McKellen is sensational as the ornery reclusive artist, and Coel is equally brilliant as the one who forces him to reckon with the unfinished works and why exactly they've been stuck in the attic for years. In a just world, McKellen would be an Oscar frontrunner here, and Ed Solomon's clever screenplay would be nominated as well. It's one of the year's very best films.

What other critics are saying: It earned incredibly strong reviews. Clarisse Loughrey at the Independent writes, "I'm certain there's a piece of [Soderbergh's] soul in The Christophers, if you look hard enough." San Francisco Chronicle's Mick LaSalle calls it "intelligent and original."

How to watch: The Christophers is now streaming on Hulu .

Why I liked it: Passenger is an extremely silly horror movie that nevertheless does exactly what it says on the tin and delivers the scary goods.

After a young couple witnesses a gruesome highway accident, they soon realize they did not leave the crash scene alone. A demonic presence that won't stop until it claims them both turns their #VanLife adventure into a nightmare. In short, it's a haunted house movie, but set in a van.

The opening scene, in particular, is incredibly effective at setting the stage for what follows; I was most impressed by how casually funny it was right off the bat, making you laugh immediately with characters you've only just met. The scene that unfolds is tense, and the cut-to-title had the crowd I saw it with screaming with delight.

You'll be checking your watch, however, any time the movie slows down to let the characters talk about their inner lives. It's not the kind of movie that requires much relationship backstory, and whenever the boyfriend gets earnest about his ambitions for his van, it's hard not to laugh at how thinly drawn they are. But all the spooky set pieces are well-constructed enough and will make you jump, so it's worth enduring the boring bits.

Norwegian filmmaker André Øvredal has yet to top his debut feature, The Autopsy of Jane Doe, but Passenger is his most fun work since that truly great horror film, after the duds The Last Voyage of the Demeter , Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark and Umma, which nobody saw.

What other critics are saying: Not everyone is as kind to genre flicks as I am, so it's more of a mixed bag. Alison Foreman at IndieWire is on my side, however, writing that it "may lack the interpersonal and mythological complexities required of a proper, obsession-worthy classic. But Øvredal is nevertheless skilled at trapping his audience inside a disorienting, semi-liminal space where anything can happen." The Guardian's Benjamin Lee was not wowed, writing, "We're never really thrust onto the road with the film, occupying a seat alongside them. Instead, we're stuck half-watching from afar, dozing our way through a journey that takes us, and the horror genre at large, back rather than forward."

How to watch: Passenger is now streaming on Paramount+ .

Mother Mary: This totally dull disappointment from David Lowery ( The Green Knight, Ain't Them Bodies Saints) is about art, you see. In a metaphorical sense. Anne Hathaway plays an iconic pop star who reunites with her estranged best friend and former costume designer, played by Michaela Coel, on the eve of her comeback performance. It's presumably meant to be a treatise on the creative process and who or what inspires the art, but its nonlinear approach and repetitiveness make it a chore to watch. "These metaphors are exhausting" is an actual line of dialogue in the film, and also functions as a succinct review! If you want to watch Michaela Coel in a movie about art, check out The Christophers, reviewed above. Now streaming on Hulu .

Buffet Infinity: This bizarre Canadian indie gem splits the difference between sketch comedy and a sprawling horror epic, weaving its wild story entirely through fake local TV commercials. It plays like a feature-length adaptation of what used to air on Cartoon Network's Adult Swim block in the middle of the night, but more nightmarish. The synopsis is as follows: A local restaurant faces the looming threat of the new dining behemoth in town: Buffet Infinity. As Buffet Infinity endlessly expands, engulfing everything in its path, a sinister conspiracy unfolds and unfathomable powers begin to seep into the vulnerable community of Westridge County, Alberta. It's easier to experience it than describe it. Now streaming on Shudder.

I Swear: This BAFTA-winning film, which you likely heard of due to the controversy at the ceremony , is now available in the U.S. on streaming, and it's charming enough to recommend even if its attempts at comedy sometimes rub up against its earnestness. The film follows the true story of John Davidson's journey from a misunderstood teenager in 1980s Britain to a present-day advocate for the understanding and acceptance of Tourette's syndrome. articles.title: We’re All Going to the World’s Fair is an intimate coming-of-age horror film
articles.summary: Now is the perfect time to revisit Jane Schoenbrun’s first film, We’re All Going to the World’s Fair, an intimate coming-of-age horror film like nothing else.
articles.body: Jane Schoenbrun’s latest film, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, is making a splash in theaters right now. So it seems like the perfect time to revisit their first film, We’re All Going to the World’s Fair. I fell in love with this film when I first saw it at Sundance in 2021.  We are immediately introduced to our protagonist, Casey, as she engages in the World’s Fair Challenge, a sort of ARG creepypasta meets ice bucket challenge. There’s a creepy mantra, some bloodletting, and a mysterious video — basically a speedrun of horror movie tropes. But having them all delivered by this young girl alone in her room who just stares directly into her webcam the whole time is unsettling. And I actually physically recoiled when she jabbed herself repeatedly with a pin to draw blood. [Media: https://youtu.be/y0AnGfzgh_w] The idea is that people perform the ritual and then they’re supposed to change in some sort of nebulous way. It’s set up as some sort of “game” where people are supposed to report their symptoms, as they turn into plastic or their guts and become Tetris pieces. Ultimately, World’s Fair is a coming-of-age story about a lonely young girl. She’s never shown talking to kids her own age. Her father is never seen, only heard, and does nothing but yell. She desperately attempts to connect with others by uploading videos documenting the changes she experiences after performing the challenge.  Importantly, unlike many other coming-of-age films, World’s Fair isn’t about Casey’s sexual awakening and avoids sexualizing her entirely. Instead, it’s about her search for belonging in an extremely online world. Basically the only other character to get any screen time is JLB, a lonely middle-aged man who claims Casey is in danger. The relationship between JLB and Casey adds another layer of unease to the film, which already blends horror elements with uncomfortably intimate glimpses into the life of a young girl. The whole thing has a voyeuristic quality. It’s never explicitly stated, but it certainly seems like JLB is attempting to groom the vulnerable Casey. The movie stews in its uncomfortable ambiguity. And that’s part of what makes it great. It may not reach the surreal or campy heights of I Saw the TV Glow or Camp Miasma, but it’s a rare indie cinema original that uses body horror tropes in new and interesting ways. We’re All Going to the World’s Fair is available to stream on Criterion Channel, Kanopy, and Hoopla.
